title: Early Bronze Age Anatolia
subtitle: 3,000–2,000 BC · Troy, the Alaca Höyük Tombs and the Tin of the Taurus

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Walled Troy, the planned towns of the northwest, the Hattian tomb-princes of the plateau and the Euphrates after the Arslantepe palace

entries.label: Troy I — a walled village at the Dardanelles
entries.hint: The first Troy was a small fortified settlement on a rocky spur above the plain of the Scamander, with stone walls, bastions and a gateway, and long, narrow houses of mudbrick on stone footings. It already looked towards the Aegean islands as much as to inland Anatolia. Nobody then called it Troy; the name belongs to a later world.
entries.note: Carl Blegen et al., Troy I–IV (Princeton, 1950–58); Manfred Korfmann and the Tübingen–Cincinnati excavations, Studia Troica (1988–).

entries.label: Demircihöyük and Küllüoba — planned towns of the northwest
entries.hint: On the Eskişehir plain, Demircihöyük was laid out as a ring of joined rectangular houses behind a fortification wall, with a central open space. Küllüoba shows a similar planned and fortified settlement with long rows of rooms. Both show communities with the organisational means to build to a plan, in a region with no known capital.
entries.note: Manfred Korfmann, Demircihöyük (Mainz, 1983–); Turan Efe on Küllüoba, excavation reports (1990s–).

entries.label: Karataş-Semayük — a Lycian town and its cemeteries
entries.hint: In the Elmalı plain of the Lycian highlands, a walled settlement of stone-founded houses and a separate cemetery of large jar burials show a community with its own pottery and burial tradition and signs of unequal wealth. Machteld Mellink's excavations (1963–71) opened this region of the southwest to the Early Bronze Age map.
entries.note: Machteld Mellink, 'Excavations at Karataş-Semayük in Lycia', American Journal of Archaeology (annual reports, 1964–71); Mellink, 'The Early Bronze Age in Southwest Anatolia' (1969).

entries.label: Troy II — the planned citadel
entries.hint: The second Troy was a citadel of some 9,000 square metres, ringed with a stone-footed mudbrick wall with gates and ramps and holding large rectangular halls on a planned layout, with lower settlement outside. The excavators' dates run from c. 2550 to c. 2300 BC. It is a regional power on the straits of the first rank, even if its ruler remains unnamed.
entries.note: Blegen, Troy I–IV (1950–58); Korfmann's reports on the lower settlement (Studia Troica, 1990s).

entries.label: Troy III–V — continuity in a poorer town
entries.hint: After the burning of Troy II the site was rebuilt in poorer form, with smaller houses on the old citadel, and Troy IV in particular was damaged by fire repeatedly. The sequence shows continuous occupation but a thinner material culture, with wheel-made pottery becoming common and Anatolian forms replacing the older Aegean-facing ones.
entries.note: Carl Blegen et al., Troy I–IV (1950–58).

entries.label: The Hattians and the name of the land
entries.hint: The people of the central plateau spoke Hattic, a language unrelated to any other known, and the land was called Hatti. Hittite scribes later kept the name and wrote down Hattic rituals, names and place names, so that the people's name survives on the very kingdom that displaced them. The entry is dated by the archaeology of the Alaca tombs, not by any text of the time.
entries.note: Hittite texts from Boğazköy preserving Hattic ritual; Harry Hoffner and Craig Melchert, A Grammar of the Hittite Language (2008) on Hattic and Hittite.

entries.label: The royal tombs of Alaca Höyük
entries.hint: At Alaca Höyük, thirteen or fourteen shaft graves, excavated in the 1930s by Hamit Koşay and Remzi Oğuz Arık, held crouched burials accompanied by gold, silver and electrum jewellery, copper-alloy weapons and vessels, and bronze sun-discs and animal standards. The dead are unnamed and left no writing; 'royal' is an interpretation of the wealth and the regalia, but it is a reasonable one.
entries.note: H. Z. Koşay and R. O. Arık, Alaca Höyük excavation reports (1935–39); Aykut Çınaroğlu, Arkhaia Anatolika (2018) on the tomb chronology.

entries.label: Horoztepe and Mahmatlar — elite graves of the Pontic hinterland
entries.hint: Further east in the Kızılırmak and Yeşilırmak valleys, tombs found at Horoztepe and Mahmatlar held metal vessels, weapons, bull standards and ornaments of similar type to Alaca's, found in part by farmers and sold before archaeologists reached them. The finds suggest several wealthy centres across the plateau rather than one.
entries.note: Tahsin Özgüç and Muzaffer Akok, Horoztepe: An Early Bronze Age Settlement and Cemetery (Ankara, 1958).

entries.label: Arslantepe after the palace — herders and the Royal Tomb
entries.hint: After the palace burned, wattle-and-daub huts and Kura-Araxes pottery now stood on the mound, with a rich cist tomb at its edge holding arsenical copper, copper-silver, silver and gold weapons, tools and ornaments with parallels in the Caucasus. The old centre reasserted itself later with a new elite, the metals of which attest to a wide network.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane, Arslantepe excavation volumes (1993–); UNESCO World Heritage listing of the Arslantepe Mound (2021).

entries.label: The Karaz and Pulur villages — the Kura-Araxes in Anatolia
entries.hint: On the Erzurum plain and in the Upper Euphrates valley, villages of round and rectangular houses with central hearths and hand-burnished black-and-red pottery appear, an eastern Anatolian branch of the Kura-Araxes or Early Transcaucasian culture. Their economy rested on mixed farming and mobile herding. They formed no state, but they linked the Caucasus to the Euphrates for five hundred years.
entries.note: Charles Burney's eastern Anatolian surveys and excavations (1950s–60s); Antonio Sagona, The Archaeology of the Caucasus (2018).

entries.label: Tarsus-Gözlükule — a walled town of Cilicia
entries.hint: Hetty Goldman's excavations at Gözlü Kule in Tarsus (1935–39) produced a deep stratigraphic sequence through the Early Bronze Age, with a walled town, planned houses and pottery in both local and Syrian traditions. Cilicia sat on the road between the Taurus and the Mediterranean and had a history of its own.
entries.note: Hetty Goldman (ed.), Excavations at Gözlü Kule, Tarsus, vol. II: From the Neolithic through the Bronze Age (Princeton, 1956).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The fire at Troy II, fortified towns, an uneven destruction horizon and Sargon's legendary march

entries.label: Fortified towns of the west and north
entries.hint: Troy, Demircihöyük, Küllüoba, Karataş-Semayük, Beycesultan and many other towns of western Anatolia were enclosed within walls with towers and gates in the Early Bronze Age II. Defence was a normal part of community life, and the walls were maintained and rebuilt for centuries.
entries.note: Manfred Korfmann (Demircihöyük reports); Machteld Mellink (Karataş); Seton Lloyd and James Mellaart, Beycesultan (1962–72).

entries.label: The burning of Troy II
entries.hint: The citadel of Troy II was destroyed by a violent fire, which left charred timbers and deep ash through the buildings. The date is placed anywhere between about 2450 and 2200 BC by different dating methods, and whether the cause was an enemy raid, an earthquake or an accident is not settled. Conclusive evidence of warfare is lacking.
entries.note: Carl Blegen, Troy I–IV (1950); Korfmann's chronology in Studia Troica (1990s); Troy chronology debates in the Troia volumes.

entries.label: The burnt towns of the late Early Bronze Age
entries.hint: Many Anatolian sites — Troy, Tarsus, Karataş, Beycesultan and others — show fire damage or abandonment between about 2300 and 2000 BC. James Mellaart read this as the arrival of the Indo-European-speaking ancestors of the Hittites. Today the horizon is seen as uneven in date and cause, with local continuity at many sites, and the invasion thesis is largely set aside.
entries.note: James Mellaart, 'Anatolia and the Indo-Europeans', Journal of Indo-European Studies 9 (1981) and earlier work; Mellaart, The Earliest Civilizations of the Near East (1965).

entries.label: Sargon at Purushanda
entries.hint: A later epic, 'The King of Battle', tells how merchants of Akkad appealed to Sargon against their treatment by Nur-Daggal, king of Purushanda in Anatolia, and how he marched across mountains to win. Copies survive from Babylonia, Amarna and the Hittite archive at Boğazköy. The campaign's historicity is uncertain, but Anatolian rulers were invoking Sargon's march 700 years later.
entries.note: J. G. Westenholz, Legends of the Kings of Akkade (1997); Hittite copy from Boğazköy (KBo III 13 and related); Hattusili I's annals alluding to Sargon.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Seals on storeroom closures and the royal words Hatti left to the Hittites

entries.label: Seals on storeroom closures
entries.hint: Numerous clay lumps bearing seal impressions — with geometric and animal designs — were used to close doors, jars and bundles at Troy II, Tarsus and other sites. The practice shows storage and distribution controlled at a defined point and a mark of identity applied to a household's or an authority's property. Writing was not yet used.
entries.note: Blegen, Troy I–IV (1950–58); Goldman, Tarsus II (1956); Troy sealings in Studia Troica.

entries.label: The royal words of Hatti
entries.hint: The Hittites of later centuries called their king the tabarna and their queen the tawananna, both words taken from Hattic. They held a Hattic ritual vocabulary of palace and cult, so that the courts of the Hattian princes were in some sense inherited. The entry rests on later texts, not on contemporary inscriptions.
entries.note: Hittite texts from Boğazköy; Harry Hoffner and Craig Melchert 2008; Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (1998).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Sun discs and animal standards, owl-faced pots, jar cemeteries and the Hattian gods

entries.label: Owl-faced vessels and idols at Troy
entries.hint: Troy I and II yielded vessels and idols with schematic human faces, large round eyes and a beak-like nose, and small flat stone idols. Schliemann read them as the owl-eyed goddess Athena; the reading belongs to the nineteenth century, not to the third millennium, and what they represented is unknown.
entries.note: Heinrich Schliemann, Ilios (1880); Blegen, Troy I–IV (1950–58).

entries.label: The jar cemeteries of the west
entries.hint: In western Anatolia the dead were laid in large storage jars (pithoi) set in cemeteries beside or apart from the settlements, adults in contracted posture in large jars up to two metres high and infants and children in smaller ones. The best-known are the Yortan cemeteries near Balıkesir and those at Karataş-Semayük. The grave goods are usually modest.
entries.note: Yortan culture literature (Kamil, UCL thesis 1980); Mellink, AJA reports on Karataş-Semayük.

entries.label: Hattic gods preserved by the Hittites
entries.hint: The Hittite state cult preserved the Hattian gods in Hattic names: the storm god Taru, the sun goddess Wurusemu of Arinna and the vanishing fertility god Telipinu, whose myths were copied by Hittite scribes. They are known only from texts of c. 1500–1200 BC, and the entry is dated by the world they preserve.
entries.note: Hittite cult texts from Boğazköy (CTH 321–330); Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994).

entries.label: Sun discs and animal standards
entries.hint: The tombs held open-work bronze discs, with crossed bars and inset animals, and standards of bulls and stags on small stands, which are read as cult objects, possibly carried on carts or poles in procession. They combine solar and animal symbolism in a way that the Hittites later took up. Their precise purpose, however, remains disputed.
entries.note: Koşay and Arık 1935–39; Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara; Çınaroğlu 2018.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Priam's Treasure, the gold of the Alaca tombs, the megaron and the two-handled cup

entries.label: Lyres on the seals
entries.hint: The earliest depictions of lyres from Anatolia and northern Syria occur on cylinder seals from Oylum Höyük, Carchemish and Urkesh, dated to the first half of the third millennium BC. The images are small and show a five- or six-string frame instrument. Music in the Anatolian record begins in these tiny scenes, not in any surviving instrument.
entries.note: Oylum Höyük seals (Engin Özgen's excavations, Kilis); Carchemish and Urkesh parallels; survey in the literature on Hittite music. Date approximate.

entries.label: The two-handled cup — the depas
entries.hint: A tall drinking vessel with two handles and a rounded base, the depas amphikypellon, was made in clay and, at Troy, in silver. It was known at Troy, Poliochni, Kusura and Kültepe and shows a common elite drinking culture over the Early Bronze Age world of western and central Anatolia and the Aegean.
entries.note: Blegen, Troy I–IV; Kusura reports (Lamb, Archaeologia 1936–37); Poliochni (Bernabò Brea, 1964–76).

entries.label: Priam's Treasure
entries.loc: Troy II · now Pushkin Museum, Moscow
entries.hint: A hoard of gold diadems, earrings, bracelets, silver vessels and weapons found by Heinrich Schliemann in 1873 in the southwestern part of the Troy II citadel. He smuggled it out of the Ottoman Empire, it was shown in Berlin, taken to Moscow in 1945 and put on public display at the Pushkin Museum in 1996. The hoard is some thousand years older than any Trojan War.
entries.note: Schliemann, Trojanische Alterthümer (1874) and Ilios (1880); Pushkin Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow.

entries.label: The megaron of Troy II
entries.hint: Troy II's citadel was laid out around large rectangular halls with a front porch and a central hearth, of mudbrick on stone, set in a regular plan. The megaron form, a long room with an open porch, would later define the palaces of the Aegean and the temples of Greece.
entries.note: Blegen, Troy I–IV (1950–58); Korfmann, Studia Troica.

entries.label: The gold and electrum of the Hattian tombs
entries.hint: The Alaca graves held gold diadems and ornaments, copper vessels, electrum and silver work, and decorated bronze standards inlaid with silver. They show a metalworking tradition, working with cast and hammered pieces, at a high level of technique before any city or writing appeared.
entries.note: Koşay and Arık, Alaca Höyük reports (1935–39); Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Who spoke Anatolian before the Hittites, what Hattic was, and the 'International Spirit'

entries.label: Who spoke Anatolian before the Hittites?
entries.hint: The Hittite, Luwian and Palaic languages belong to the Indo-European family, but where and when their speakers arrived is disputed — via the Caucasus, the Balkans or an Anatolian homeland. Ancient DNA from Bronze Age Anatolia shows no major steppe ancestry in the Hittite-period population, which has weighed against steppe-origin models for the Anatolian branch.
entries.note: Peter Damgaard et al., Science 360 (2018); Iosif Lazaridis et al., 'The genetic history of the Southern Arc', Science 377 (2022); the Indo-European homeland debate.

entries.label: The 'International Spirit'
entries.hint: Colin Renfrew coined the 'International Spirit' for the shared metalwork, pottery shapes, seals and drinking vessels linking the Aegean, western Anatolia and the Near East in the Early Bronze Age. Rather than a single empire, he argued, a network of regional societies in contact had adopted similar forms. The idea remains a standard way to read the period.
entries.note: Colin Renfrew, The Emergence of Civilisation (1972).

entries.label: Hattic — a language preserved by its conquerors
entries.hint: Hattic has no known relatives. It survives only in religious texts of the Hittite archives, where the Hattic words are given with Hittite translations. The Hittite scribes treated it as a sacred language of ritual, one reason it was written down at all.
entries.note: Hittite texts at Boğazköy with Hattic passages; Annelies Kammenhuber, Hattisch (1969); Hoffner and Melchert 2008.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The tin workings of the Taurus and a wool economy beside the herding of the Kura-Araxes

entries.label: The tin workings of the Taurus
entries.hint: At Kestel in the Bolkar range an ancient mine, and at Göltepe a small walled settlement with crucible slags rich in tin, were claimed by Aslıhan Yener's team as the first tin mining and processing in the Near East, with radiocarbon dates from the late fourth to the late third millennium BC. The attribution has been challenged: the tin content is low and some argue the mine was for gold. The question of where early bronze got its tin is still open.
entries.note: K. A. Yener et al., Antiquity 61 (1987) and American Journal of Archaeology 97 (1993) (exchange with J. D. Muhly); Yener, The Domestication of Metals (2000); Minerals 11 (2021) review.

entries.label: Mobile herding and the Kura-Araxes
entries.hint: The Kura-Araxes villages and the settlers on the Arslantepe mound after the palace were mixed farmers and mobile herders, with transhumance between winter villages and summer pastures in the highlands. The herders' economy was a quiet but effective one: it filled the region from the Caucasus to the Malatya plain with small, flexible communities.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane (ed.), Arslantepe volumes; Frangipane, Origini 34 (2012); Sagona 2018.

entries.label: Wool, whorls and the cloth economy
entries.hint: Troy and other Early Bronze Age towns yielded spindle whorls and loom weights in large numbers, and on Sherratt's argument wool-bearing sheep become important in this period. Wool and cloth were a regular product of household labour and a probable item of exchange with neighbours. Andrew Sherratt's 'secondary products revolution' places the change in the fourth and third millennia.
entries.note: Blegen, Troy I–IV; Andrew Sherratt, 'Plough and pastoralism', in Pattern of the Past (1981).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Tin bronze, the stone-and-mudbrick citadel, the potter's wheel and lost-wax casting

entries.label: The walls and ramps of Troy
entries.hint: The Troy II citadel wall was built of mudbrick on a high stone socle, with projecting towers and monumental gateways reached by paved ramps. Its builders planned drainage, floors and gates in one design. Defensive architecture of this scale needed a ruler able to draw labour for years.
entries.note: Blegen, Troy I–IV (1950–58); Korfmann reports.

entries.label: Tin bronze at Troy
entries.hint: Analysis of weapons and ornaments from Troy II shows copper alloyed with tin in proportions that make a true bronze, beside arsenical copper. The shift across the third millennium to tin bronze required a dependable supply of a metal found in only a few places, which is why the question of tin sources matters.
entries.note: Metal analyses of Troy finds (Studia Troica and the Stuttgart analysis series, 1960s–); Yener 2000.

entries.label: The potter's wheel reaches the west
entries.hint: Wheel-made pottery appears in western Anatolia in the middle of the third millennium BC, and Mellink and Blegen proposed that it came by sea. It is a sharp break in how pots were made, since wheel throwing replaced hand-building and made craft production faster and more standardised. Not every region took it up at the same time.
entries.note: Blegen, Troy I–IV; Mellink, American Journal of Archaeology reports; Murat Türkteki (2012) on the debate.

entries.label: Cast standards of the Hattian smiths
entries.hint: The bull and stag standards, and the sun discs of the Alaca tombs, were cast in complex shapes, then finished by hammering and inlay with silver. Casting with moulds of several parts was demanding and shows specialised smiths who were supported by the princes who wore and displayed their work.
entries.note: Koşay and Arık 1935–39; Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Troy and the Aegean, the Caucasus road to the Euphrates and the lapis of Troy

entries.label: Troy and the Aegean islands
entries.hint: Troy I and II share pottery shapes, house plans and burial customs with Poliochni on Lemnos, Thermi on Lesbos and the settlements of the Cyclades. The Troad was a link in an island-hopping chain between the Aegean and the interior of Anatolia, well placed for traffic through the straits.
entries.note: Bernabò Brea, Poliochni (1964–76); Korfmann on Troy and the Aegean (Studia Troica).

entries.label: The Caucasus road to the Euphrates
entries.hint: The metals in the Arslantepe cist tomb and the pottery of the Karaz and Pulur villages match types from the Caucasus. Goods, metalworking knowledge and people moved from the South Caucasus along the upland valleys to the Euphrates, in the first long-distance network of the highlands.
entries.note: Frangipane (ed.) Arslantepe series; Sagona 2018.

entries.label: Lapis and carnelian at Troy
entries.hint: The Troy II treasures are reported to include lapis lazuli beads and other imported stones, and stone mace-heads and axes of fine hard stone. The lapis came from the mines of Badakhshan in the far northeast of Afghanistan, which makes the Troad the westernmost known end of a trade stretching across the Iranian plateau.
entries.note: Schliemann, Ilios (1880); Blegen, Troy I–IV; lapis sourcing literature (Casanova, Le lapis-lazuli, 1992).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A short drought and the end of the Early Bronze Age

entries.label: A short drought and its uneven reach
entries.hint: Around 2200 BC records from the eastern Mediterranean and Mesopotamia show a century or two of drier conditions, and the collapse of the Akkadian state is often linked to it. How far Anatolia felt it is uncertain. Some towns burned or were abandoned, but others carried on, and local politics weigh as much as rainfall.
entries.note: Harvey Weiss et al., Science 261 (1993); Anatolian pollen and speleothem records; the 4.2 ka event literature.

entries.label: The end of the Early Bronze Age
entries.hint: By around 2000 BC many of the walled towns of the west had been abandoned or reduced, the Hattian tombs had ceased and a new, far more urban pattern emerged on the central plateau in which Assyrian merchants set up trading colonies. The shift is a cultural and political reorganisation, not a simple invasion.
entries.note: Machteld Mellink and others on the EBA III–MBA transition; Mogens Larsen, The Old Assyrian City-State and Its Colonies (1976).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Children in jars and rich and poor in the same cemetery

entries.label: Children in jars
entries.hint: Infants and children of the western jar cemeteries were set in their own smaller jars, often among the adults, and some with small pots or beads. Their treatment as members of the community, with their own burial vessels, is direct evidence of how the young were valued.
entries.note: T. Kamil, Yortan Cemetery in the Early Bronze Age of Western Anatolia (BAR, 1982).

entries.label: Rich and poor in one cemetery
entries.hint: The Karataş cemeteries, spread over several centuries, held plain jar burials with a few pots and burials with metal, ornaments and imported goods. Machteld Mellink saw there the beginnings of social stratification in the southwest: some people and families had access to goods others did not.
entries.note: Machteld Mellink, American Journal of Archaeology reports on Karataş-Semayük (1964–71); University of Pennsylvania Museum Elmalı records.
